gates.title: Eval allowance budgets: strict cap or observed stop threshold?
gates.body: B is accepted from source bd5fa3a29bb143669ea084f5ef49f218: full evaluation scope with 10% per allowance bucket/cycle. Decision needed: how to enforce that cap when a provider exposes percentage usage/reset observations but no guaranteed per-request allowance charge. Why it matters: checking after a call can detect an overshoot only after consumption; concurrent product calls and delayed readings also make attribution uncertain. A: Keep a strict cap and fail closed on routes without a defensible pre-call upper bound; continue local harness/planner and grade storage independently. Pro: preserves the approved ceiling and product headroom. Con: some allowance routes remain unevaluated until a usable bound exists. B: Treat 10% as an observed stop threshold, with sequential bounded calls and fresh readings before/after each call; stop on missing/stale readings or threshold crossing. Pro: permits sampling percentage-only providers. Con: a call or reporting delay can overshoot 10%, and shared product consumption cannot reliably be separated. Recommendation: A, because B changes the approved allowance boundary. This does not reopen full-scope approval or authorize metered spend. Question: A (strict cap with unsupported routes deferred), or B (accept the overshoot risk of an observed threshold)?
options: A: Strict cap; defer routes without bounds
B: Observed threshold; accept overshoot risk

gates.title: Host-side proxy: filtered direct connection or isolated-network relay?
gates.body:
Decision needed: connection containment for the accepted B host-side inference proxy (source 98654698af0b458492b0bb74ddd3c5e3). B remains accepted; this does not reopen container versus host deployment.
Why it matters: the proven internal/isolated worker network blocks host listeners. Host-gateway address mapping does not itself restrict destination ports. Bearer authentication protects the inference endpoint, not other host services. Native host-side containment has not been proved.
D: Filtered direct host connection. Pro: direct HTTP follows the original brief and avoids a relay. Con: platform-specific filtering, potentially privileged setup and rollback, plus IPv4/IPv6 bypass proof; hostname mapping alone is insufficient.
R: Host-initiated relay on the isolated worker network. Pro: preserves worker isolation from host listeners while keeping provider credentials/admission on the host. Con: adds a relay protocol/component and bounded mediation, cancellation and cleanup work; exact transport needs design.
Technical recommendation: R, because it preserves the proved worker network and avoids relying on new host-wide filtering. This recommendation is not an owner decision.
Question: approve R, or select D with network-policy setup scope? What constraint drives the choice?
AI next: implement the selected connection, prove positive synthetic inference and negative host/public/DNS/foreign-run access and lifecycle cleanup, then perform separately admitted provider acceptance. Keep source 98654698 open until proved. See docs/decisions/ADR-095-provider-neutral-worktree-write-isolation.md, host-side section.
Instruction audit: AGENTS.md and docs/workflow.md already require each option's pros AND cons and a recommendation. The original brief failed those rules; file-brief.py validates option count, not semantic completeness.

gates.body:
Accepted D for delivery AI; C preferred for client-product AI subject to client choice. Source 1ce80f7f35a74b09b60ea01a4fd9e7d4 is closed. No new default decision requested.

# P7 Track 2.3: AI-cost handling - reconciled alternatives

Reconciled 2026-11-27 under inbox `52b91c6139f646608224b185a775fbcf` A.
Original proposal: commit `78019a48b70a13d8847374aa6dc0eadd8bdb7fab`.

## Accepted decision and remaining boundaries

Source `1ce80f7f35a74b09b60ea01a4fd9e7d4` selected D with clarification:
our code-factory AI is our operating cost within the fixed scoped delivery fee,
never a separate client charge. Attribution is advisory for estimates and margins;
it may inform price and useful disclosure. For a client AI-enabled product,
C (client-owned keys/credits and direct provider billing) is preferred, subject
to the client's choice. Onboarding help does not transfer account responsibility.
Conditional product extraction depends on discovery demand, not immediate build
approval. The [accepted decision](decisions/p7-track23-ai-cost-handling.md)
controls over the original proposal.

The table retains historical alternatives, not pending default choices. Its
production-consumption mechanics must never be applied as delivery-AI charges.
No prices, spending, billing implementation, hard caps, credentials, external
routing, client terms or publication are authorized here.

## Viable alternatives

| Option | Pros | Cons / operational burden |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: At-cost pass-through with visible usage reports | Client pays actual attributable consumption; avoids hidden risk premium; supports changing workloads without repeated allowance negotiations. | Client total varies and reports alone do not prevent surprise bills; founder fronts spend and reconciles invoices, currency, credits and disputed usage. A separate agreed ceiling/escalation rule is still advisable. |
| B: Capped allowance with pause before overage | Predictable maximum authorized spend per agreed period; clear consent for more spending; bounds founder exposure and fits small initial pilots. | Service can pause and deadlines can move; estimation, alerts, admission controls, in-flight reservations and reconciliation are needed. An included allowance creates under-use/over-use economics that must be defined. |
| C: Client-owned provider account, directly billed; separate integration/support fee | Client controls provider invoices, budgets and continuity after handoff; founder avoids financing/reselling inference; clean cost separation. | Client onboarding, account eligibility and billing remain work; delegated credentials and usage visibility require care. Provider bills still vary; client-side caps and support responsibilities must be agreed. Credentials must not be casually shared. |
| D: Fixed bundled price for a tightly defined workload | Simplest client bill and strongest predictable fee within scope; rewards efficient delivery and removes small per-call billing disputes. | Founder absorbs consumption volatility and must price contingency; narrow volume/model/context limits and change control are essential. Unlimited usage is unsuitable without reliable economics; measuring margins still takes work. |

Prepaid credits are a funding mechanism for A/B, not a distinct cost-allocation
model: they reduce receivables but add balance, expiry, refund and tax accounting.
Metered cost-plus is also viable when a managed-service margin is explicit:
it funds operations but retains variable bills and adds markup disputes; prefer
a separate visible management fee initially. Local inference can reduce external
metering, but hardware, electricity, maintenance and capacity remain real costs;
it is a deployment choice under any option, not free consumption.

## Historical production-only mechanics - conditional, not approved

The following describes B only if separately negotiated for a client product.
It is not the selected delivery policy or an implementation requirement.

For B, recommend a separately disclosed, project-specific production budget,
actual-cost drawdown with reports, and no automatic overage purchase. State whether
it is prepaid or invoiced in arrears; recommend prepaid for initial pilots with
unused funds reconciled/refunded, subject to accountant/legal review. Do not imply
that a usage estimate is an invoice or that a provider credit is cash expenditure.

Before quoting, specify period/reset/time zone, currency/FX date and fees, taxes,
provider/tool/storage charges included, credits/refunds, failed calls/retries,
abuse liability, attribution, report cadence and dispute process. Recommend
monthly reporting plus a warning before exhaustion; exact budget and warning
threshold remain client-specific, not selected here. Reports should show period,
route/model, attributable usage, estimated versus reconciled cost, remaining
budget and adjustments, without exposing prompts or other clients' information.

Pause admission early enough to reserve worst-case in-flight costs across retries
and fallback routes; if cost cannot be bounded, do not promise a hard ceiling.
Pause AI-dependent operations safely, preserve pending work, explain timeline
effects and require explicit authorized budget increase before resuming. Critical
uninterrupted workloads need a separately agreed reserve or continuity plan.
Provider limits supplement, rather than prove, application-level protection.
Existing tracking is a starting point; no end-to-end client billing or hard-cap
enforcement was tested by this documentation task.

Illustration only, not a quote: a 200-unit monthly budget and 80-unit actual usage
means 80 attributable units under A/B/C; under B the balance treatment follows
the agreed reconciliation rule. At 260 units of requested usage B pauses admission
before the authorized 200-unit exposure is exceeded; a provider invoice or delayed
estimate is not sufficient enforcement. Under D the founder bears permitted
in-scope consumption within the fixed bundle price.

## Resolution and review boundary

The original recommendation of B as the initial default is superseded by D for
our delivery AI and the separate C preference for client-product AI. Do not ask
the owner to select the default again. Client-specific scope, cost allocation,
accountant/legal and data terms still require review before a quote, promise or
charge. The original gate `p7-track23-ai-cost-terms` records the resolved choice.

Provider references in original commit 78019a4 are historical research, not
revalidated by this reconciliation. They establish no current account allowance
or Workbench budget guarantee. See the provider source-state reference before
relying on provider behaviour.

Reconciled 2026-11-27 under inbox `52b91c6139f646608224b185a775fbcf` A.
Original proposal: commit `78019a48b70a13d8847374aa6dc0eadd8bdb7fab`.

## Accepted general intent and pending terms

Source `2c9efe65437b493792497d4f807570e0` selected B as general intent:
a broad nonexclusive deliverable licence, retaining reusable templates, with
clients free to choose who maintains and expands their software. The owner wants
both sides to benefit from existing work and to avoid forced dependency.
A/C/D remain negotiable for particular clients. The source/inspection/modification
package, niche comparison and final legal wording remain pending under existing
follow-up `6dea3d6d42ef463aaac822135748a8ed`, gate
`p7-track24-source-continuity`. B does not itself settle source access or grant
rights to all Workbench internals. No assignment, contract, price or publication
is authorized. The accepted source answer controls over this historical proposal.

## Viable alternatives

| Option | Pros / client rights | Cons / cost and reuse burden |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A: Assign bespoke deliverables; retain named background assets with sufficient embedded-use licence | Client owns agreed bespoke economic rights and can maintain/commission changes; founder retains Workbench, reusable templates and lawful general know-how. Balanced fit for custom fixed-price builds. | Requires an accurate asset schedule and rights chain. Client ownership does not automatically supply rights to embedded tooling; licence and source handoff must avoid dependency traps. Assigned bespoke code cannot simply be reused by founder. |
| B: Founder retains deliverable ownership; broad nonexclusive client licence | Founder can reuse generic implementation and amortize development, potentially reducing price; client can receive durable use, modification, third-party maintenance and deployment rights. | Some clients/procurement require ownership; client needs strong continuity/transfer rights and confidence against lock-in. Founder must distinguish reusable code from confidential client material. Wider rights and support still cost money. |
| C: Exclusive licence for named bespoke elements, with background carve-outs | Client gets defined competitive exclusivity without a full assignment; field/territory/time restrictions can target a real commercial need. | Exclusivity reduces founder reuse and merits a premium; defining reserved uses and overlaps adds negotiation and monitoring. Client still relies on licence durability; Polish formalities and duration/termination need review. |
| D: Buyout of specifically scheduled bespoke plus reusable components, where rights permit | Client gains strongest control over purchased assets and can reduce supplier dependence; suitable when strategic exclusivity has real value. | Highest price should reflect lost reuse/replacement cost; founder may impair other projects. Cannot assign third-party rights not owned, or already-granted rights away. A broad Workbench buyout needs a separate owner decision and cannot be implied by this option. |

Hosted subscription/access-only delivery is another viable service model: it can
fund ongoing operations and avoid deployment work, but gives the client less
source/continuity control, creates hosting/support/data duties and changes the
offering. Defer it as the default custom-build arrangement; use a separate scope
decision if a client actually wants hosted access rather than a delivered system.

## Required boundary and client-rights schedule

For the selected B intent, prepare a per-project rights schedule for review;
the following are candidate terms, not approved rights:

- Bespoke deliverables: named source code, configurations, designs, documentation
  and client-specific workflows. Define the proposed licence scope and effective event; any assignment
  belongs to a separately negotiated A/D alternative, not default B.
- Background assets: pre-existing Workbench, libraries, templates and reusable
  improvements specifically identified before delivery. New generic improvements
  need explicit classification; calling everything a template is insufficient.
- Embedded background rights: propose nonexclusive, worldwide, fully paid rights
  intended to survive the engagement, sufficient to run, copy, deploy, modify and
  engage replacement maintainers for the delivered system. Define affiliate,
  successor/transfer and sublicensing rights and any standalone resale limits.
  Counsel must translate intended durability into enforceable duration/termination
  terms; do not promise an irrevocable licence without review.
- Source/runbook/access handoff and dependency inventory: identify anything only
  hosted by the founder, required build tools and any proprietary dependency that
  would prevent independent operation. Owning output does not grant access to all
  Workbench internals. Agree the necessary handoff before contracting.
- Third-party/open-source assets, fonts, content and AI-assisted material: list
  provenance, licences, notices, restrictions and review evidence; do not promise
  exclusivity or assign rights that the founder does not hold. Assess copyleft and
  provider terms per component and use, not by blanket assurance.
- Client data, marks and confidential processes remain separately protected.
  Retained know-how means general skills and nonconfidential methods; it never
  permits copying client secrets, personal data or confidential code into another
  project, training corpus or portfolio. Portfolio permission is separate.

## Resolution and review boundary

The original recommendation of A is superseded by the owner's B general intent.
Do not reopen the default question. A may suit a buyer requiring bespoke ownership
but reduces founder reuse; C trades targeted exclusivity for additional price and
negotiation; D requires separately valuing lost reuse and checking owned rights.
B supports reuse and client choice but still needs a credible continuity package.
The existing source-continuity follow-up owns that unresolved decision.

Asset boundaries, confidentiality, third-party rights and legal review remain
required before client use. Counsel must review actual licence scope, form,
duration/termination and modification/maintenance terms. This reconciliation
makes no new legal finding and does not validate the original proposal's legal
sources or approve its candidate rights schedule. Original gate
`p7-track24-ip-terms` records resolved general intent, not final client terms.
